# Productivity and Impact Indicators

## Learning objectives {#indicators-objectives}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

- Compute sample h- and g-indices and distinguish a corpus publication span from an author career
- Explain the difference between size-dependent and size-independent indicators
- Explain the external reference sets needed for MNCS and PP(top 10%), and diagnose misleading within-sample normalization
- Articulate the limitations of each indicator and the risks of misuse, citing the Leiden Manifesto

## Setup {#indicators-setup}

```{r}
#| label: 10-setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openalexR)
library(glue)
library(gt)

set.seed(20260509)

source(here::here("R", "api_helpers.R"))
source(here::here("R", "utils.R"))
source(here::here("R", "sci_palette.R"))
```

## Conceptual background {#indicators-background}

Quantitative indicators are central to research evaluation — and among the most contested tools in science policy. The h-index, proposed by @hirsch2005, counts the number *h* of an author's papers that have each received at least *h* citations. Its simplicity made it wildly popular, but also obscures important nuances: it conflates productivity with impact, is insensitive to highly cited papers, and can only increase over a career [@waltman2016].

The **g-index** [@egghe2006] addresses the insensitivity to top-cited papers by requiring that the top *g* papers have together received at least *g*² citations. The **m-quotient** divides the h-index by career length, offering a rough age correction.

These are all *raw* indicators. Citation distributions differ across fields, so comparisons require a justified reference and **field normalization**. The **Mean Normalized Citation Score** (MNCS) divides each paper's citations by the world average for its field and publication year [@waltman2012mncs]. The **PP(top 10%)** — the proportion of an entity's papers in the top 10% most cited in their field — is a percentile-based indicator recommended by the Leiden Ranking.

The Leiden Manifesto [@hicks2015] and the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment [@dora2012] both caution against mechanical use of any single indicator. Indicators should support, not replace, qualitative judgement.

## Worked example {#indicators-example}

### Acquiring sample data

We fetch a sample of works and their citation counts from OpenAlex.

```{r}
#| label: 10-fetch-indicator-data
#| cache: true
works <- fetch_openalex(
  entity = "works",
  primary_location.source.id = "S148561398",
  from_publication_date = "2018-01-01",
  to_publication_date = "2023-12-31",
  options = list(sample = 500, seed = 42)
)

works_slim <- works |>
  select(id, display_name, publication_date, cited_by_count, doi) |>
  mutate(year = year(publication_date))

summary(works_slim$cited_by_count)
```

### Computing the h-index

```{r}
#| label: 10-compute-h-index
h <- compute_h_index(works_slim$cited_by_count)
cat(glue("h-index for this corpus: {h}\n"))
```

The sample h-index means that at least `r h` sampled papers each have at least `r h` citations. It is not an author career h-index.

### Computing the g-index

```{r}
#| label: 10-compute-g-index
compute_g_index <- function(citations) {
  sorted <- sort(citations, decreasing = TRUE)
  cumsum_cites <- cumsum(sorted)
  g_candidates <- which(cumsum_cites >= seq_along(sorted)^2)
  if (length(g_candidates) == 0) return(0L)
  as.integer(max(g_candidates))
}

g <- compute_g_index(works_slim$cited_by_count)
cat(glue("g-index for this corpus: {g}\n"))
```

### Publication span is not career length

A proper m-quotient needs an identified author and a justified career-start date.
This corpus contains many authors, so its publication span cannot supply that
denominator. The following h/span ratio is only a descriptive calculation.

```{r}
#| label: 10-compute-m-quotient
career_years <- as.numeric(
  difftime(max(works_slim$publication_date),
           min(works_slim$publication_date),
           units = "days")
) / 365.25

h_per_span <- if (is.finite(career_years) && career_years > 0) h / career_years else NA_real_
cat(glue("Sample h/publication-span ratio: {round(h_per_span, 3)} (span {round(career_years, 1)} years)\n"))
```

### A normalization diagnostic: using the sample as its own reference

MNCS requires a justified field/year reference with compatible document types
and citation windows. The live corpus here supplies no such reference. To show
why that matters, compute a mean within each sample year and divide the same
records by it. Every usable year must average to 1 by construction. These are
observed sample means, not simulated field means or world averages.

```{r}
#| label: 10-compute-mncs
sample_means_by_year <- works_slim |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(sample_mean = mean(cited_by_count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

works_normalized <- works_slim |>
  left_join(sample_means_by_year, by = "year") |>
  mutate(ncs = field_normalize(cited_by_count, sample_mean))

sample_ratio <- mean(works_normalized$ncs, na.rm = TRUE)
cat(glue("Mean within-sample/year ratio: {round(sample_ratio, 3)}\n"))
```

A value of 1 here is an arithmetic identity, not evidence of world-average
impact. Zero-mean years have undefined ratios and are excluded. An actual MNCS
interpretation requires an independently justified field/year reference
[@waltman2012mncs].

### Within-sample upper-percentile membership

```{r}
#| label: 10-compute-pp-top10
works_with_pct <- works_normalized |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    pct_rank = percent_rank(cited_by_count),
    is_top10 = pct_rank >= 0.90
  ) |>
  ungroup()

pp_top10 <- mean(works_with_pct$is_top10, na.rm = TRUE)
cat(glue("Share at or above the sample/year 90th percentile rank: {scales::percent(pp_top10, accuracy = 0.1)}\n"))
```

The ranks use only sampled works in each year. Ties and small groups can make
the selected share differ from 10%; a singleton has no percentile rank. This
is not field-normalized PP(top 10%). Report the ranking and tie rule explicitly.

### Visualization

```{r}
#| label: 10-fig-indicators-citation-dist
#| fig-cap: "Citation distribution of sampled works, with the h-index threshold marked."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of citation counts with a vertical dashed line at the h-index value, showing the long-tailed distribution typical of citation data."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
works_slim |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cited_by_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = palette_sci(1), color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = h, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = h + 5, y = Inf, label = glue("h = {h}"),
           vjust = 2, hjust = 0, color = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Citation count", y = "Number of works") +
  theme_sci()
```

```{r}
#| label: 10-fig-indicators-mncs-by-year
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic: each usable sample/year normalizes to its own mean of one."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart at one across usable years, demonstrating the arithmetic identity created by normalizing each sample year to itself."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
works_normalized |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(sample_ratio = mean(ncs, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = sample_ratio)) +
  geom_line(color = palette_sci(1), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = palette_sci(1), size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Within-sample/year ratio") +
  theme_sci()
```

### Summary table

```{r}
#| label: 10-tbl-indicators-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of computed indicators."
tibble(
  Indicator = c("Sample h-index", "Sample g-index", "Sample h/span", "Mean sample/year ratio", "Sample upper-percentile share"),
  Value = c(
    as.character(h),
    as.character(g),
    round(h_per_span, 3) |> as.character(),
    round(sample_ratio, 3) |> as.character(),
    scales::percent(pp_top10, accuracy = 0.1)
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    glue("{h} papers with >= {h} citations each"),
    glue("Top {g} papers have >= {g}^2 = {g^2} cumulative citations"),
    "Not a career m-quotient",
    "One by construction; not MNCS",
    "Within-sample rank rule; not world PP(top 10%)"
  )
) |>
  gt()
```

## Diagnostics and interpretation {#indicators-diagnostics}

When interpreting bibliometric indicators, keep in mind:

- **Citation windows matter.** Recent papers have had less time to accumulate citations. The MNCS accounts for this by normalizing within publication year, but raw h-index and g-index do not.
- **Field differences.** A "good" h-index in mathematics differs vastly from one in biomedicine. Only compare within fields, or use field-normalized indicators.
- **Size dependence.** The h-index grows with the number of papers published. Comparing researchers at different career stages or with different publication rates requires the m-quotient or percentile indicators.
- **Self-citations.** None of the indicators above exclude self-citations. In a full analysis, consider computing variants with and without self-citations.

## Limitations and responsible use {#indicators-limitations}

<div class="callout callout-warn">
## Limitations and responsible use

No single number can capture the quality, significance, or societal impact of a researcher's work. The Leiden Manifesto [@hicks2015] offers ten principles for the responsible use of metrics:

1. Quantitative evaluation should support, not replace, expert assessment.
2. Measure performance against the research missions of the institution, group, or researcher.
3. Protect excellence in locally relevant research (not just globally visible research).
4. Keep data collection and analytical processes open, transparent, and simple.
5. Allow those being evaluated to verify data and analysis.

The h-index in particular can be gamed through self-citation, salami slicing, or guest authorship. It penalises researchers in small fields, those who publish fewer but higher-impact works, and those who take career breaks. The DORA declaration [@dora2012] explicitly warns against using journal-level metrics (like the Impact Factor) as surrogates for individual article quality — but the same caution applies to any single indicator.

**Always present multiple indicators alongside qualitative context.** Never use a single number to make hiring, promotion, or funding decisions.
</div>

## Common pitfalls {#indicators-pitfalls}

<div class="callout callout-stop">
## Common pitfalls

- **Comparing h-indices across fields.** A physicist with h = 40 and a mathematician with h = 15 may have equivalent standing in their respective fields. Use field-normalized indicators for cross-field comparisons.
- **Ignoring the citation window.** Computing MNCS without accounting for publication year conflates old, well-cited papers with recent ones that haven't had time to accumulate citations.
- **Using the wrong denominator for PP(top 10%).** The "top 10%" must be defined relative to the same field and year, not relative to your own corpus.
- **Reporting precision that isn't there.** An MNCS of 1.237 vs. 1.241 is not a meaningful difference. Report with appropriate precision and always provide confidence intervals or bootstrapped uncertainty where possible.
</div>

## Exercises {#indicators-exercises}

1. **Career h-index.** Fetch all works by a specific author using `oa_fetch(entity = "works", author.id = "...")`. Compute their h-index, g-index, and m-quotient. How do the three indicators tell different stories about the same career?

2. **Self-citation sensitivity.** If you could identify self-citations (e.g., via author overlap in the reference list), how would removing them affect the h-index? Write pseudocode for this analysis.

3. **Empirical resampling.** Resample the within-sample/year ratios while holding their empirical reference fixed. Explain why the resulting interval does not measure uncertainty about world-normalized MNCS.

4. **Normalization and ranks.** Compare each year's mean sample ratio with its upper-percentile share. Explain why the ratio is fixed at one and why ties can change the percentile share; neither ranks world-normalized impact.

## Further reading {#indicators-reading}

- @hirsch2005 — The original h-index paper.
- @egghe2006 — The g-index, addressing the h-index's insensitivity to highly cited papers.
- @waltman2016 — A comprehensive review of citation impact indicators and their properties.
- @waltman2012mncs — The theoretical basis for the MNCS ("new crown indicator").
- @hicks2015 — The Leiden Manifesto: ten principles for responsible metrics.
- @dora2012 — DORA: the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment.
